sections.html:
Cheyenne is Wyoming's capital and the seat of Laramie County, in the far southeast corner of the state. It stands at about 6,086 feet on Crow Creek and Dry Creek and covers a little over 32 square miles. The 2025 population estimate is 66,507. Two interstates meet southwest of town: I-25 runs north to south, I-80 east to west, and I-180 loops through the city along US 85. Cheyenne Regional Airport has daily nonstop United Express flights to Denver, and the Cheyenne Transit Program runs local buses.

Government, transportation, the military and a growing technology sector carry the economy. State offices, Union Pacific and BNSF rail yards, and F.E. Warren Air Force Base are long-standing anchors, and Microsoft, Meta, Magpul, Searing Industries and Eagle Claw are major employers. Cheyenne Regional, the local hospital, reports more than 2,000 employees. Sellers who work for the base or a large employer may need to move on a short timeline after a transfer or job change.

The city has several historic districts, and homes inside them may face extra review:

  • Downtown Cheyenne Historic District
  • Lakeview Historic District
  • Rainsford Historic District
  • Capitol North Historic District
  • South Side Historic District

If your house sits inside one of these areas, ask the city's Planning and Development office what applies before you spend money on repairs.

Cheyenne is cold and semiarid, with strong summer thunderstorms, and hail does the most harm to a roof. The National Weather Service counts more than 6 days a year with severe hail of an inch or larger nearby, with June the busiest month and July next. Quarter-size hail is the most common report. It can fall anywhere from March into October, mostly late in the afternoon.

  • Annual precipitation is about 15.9 inches, mostly from May through August.
  • Seasonal snowfall averages about 60 inches, with March and April the snowiest months.
  • Lows reach 0 degrees Fahrenheit on roughly nine mornings a year.

Buyers and inspectors look closely at shingles, gutters, siding and furnace age. A roof with visible hail bruising can lower an offer or stall a financed sale. A cash buyer who purchases as is does not ask you to fix that first.

Flood risk is a real topic because of the flash flood of August 1, 1985. The National Weather Service recorded 6.06 inches of rain in about three hours, 12 deaths, 70 injuries and more than $61 million in damage. A FEMA report afterward called for better stormwater and floodplain management, and the city put new drainage plans and retention projects in place in the late 1980s.

Today the city's Engineering Services Department keeps flood insurance rate maps and base flood elevations. Find it at 2101 O'Neil Ave., Room 206, or call (307) 637-6268. If your home is near Crow Creek or Dry Creek, check the map before you list. A buyer's lender may require flood insurance, and finding that out late can cost you days.

sections.h2: Permits and code rules before a sale
sections.html:
Cheyenne requires a permit for many repairs sellers consider, including reroofing, decks, garages, water heaters, and electrical, plumbing and HVAC work. Review can take up to 10 business days, and fees are based on project value.

Some smaller jobs are exempt. A detached shed under 200 square feet needs no permit, and flatwork such as a concrete patio generally does not, unless it is in the city right-of-way. Fences over 6 feet need a permit, and the city limits fences to 4 feet in front of the house.

  • Carports over 200 square feet, or attached to another structure, need a permit.
  • Zoning violations can carry fines of $100 per day.
  • Structures built in a setback may have to be removed.

Short-term rentals are treated like other residential uses, so there is no separate registration, but each rental must hold the approvals it needs. If you have an unpermitted deck, shed or carport, call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 before a buyer finds it in an inspection.

Laramie County bills property tax in two halves. The Laramie County Treasurer is at 309 W. 20th Street, Cheyenne.

PaymentPayable byIf unpaid
First halfNovember 10Interest on this half is waived if you pay the whole bill by December 31
Second halfMay 10 of the following yearDelinquent, with 18 percent interest per year

A bill still unpaid on May 11 goes onto a delinquent list certified by the treasurer, and the county holds a lien that can lead to a tax sale.

Property is assessed to the owner of record on January 1. If you bought or recorded a deed after that date, the notice may not carry your name, but you still owe the tax. The assessor mails schedules no later than the fourth Monday in April, and you have 30 days from the mailing to file a written objection. Our Wyoming property tax guide covers appeals in more detail.

A deed for a Cheyenne sale is recorded with the Laramie County Clerk, which cannot accept it until a sworn statement of the price and terms is filed. W.S. 34-1-142 makes that statement confidential, so the sale price does not become a public record.

The clerk's recording fee is $12 for the first page and $3 for each additional page, and documents with several legal descriptions carry an added $15.50 administrative fee. The office is at 309 W 20th St, Suite 1600, and takes e-recording through several vendors. Hours are Monday through Friday, 8:00 AM to 5:00 PM.

Plan on the title company paying any open tax from your proceeds before the deed is filed, so ask the treasurer for the current balance early.

sections.h2: How does a cash sale work in Cheyenne?
sections.html:
With a cash sale a buyer purchases your house without a lender, so the deal does not depend on an appraisal or loan approval. You tell us about the property, we review it, and you decide whether the offer works for you.

This route often suits sellers in one of these situations:

  • An inherited house that needs probate paperwork and cleanout
  • A hail-damaged roof or older systems that would fail a lender's inspection
  • A military or job move with a fixed date
  • Back taxes or a payment problem that is getting worse

We buy as is, with no commission and no closing costs charged to you, and you owe nothing if you decline an offer. Call or text (424) 435-2326 or use the form on this page to start.

faqs.q: How fast can I sell my house in Cheyenne?
faqs.a: A cash sale can close faster than a listing because it skips lender approval and appraisal. The timeline still depends on title work, any probate, and the date you choose. Tell us your deadline and we will work around it.

faqs.q: Do I need to fix hail damage before selling in Cheyenne?
faqs.a: Not if you sell to a cash buyer who purchases as is. If you list on the open market, a hail-damaged roof often comes up in the inspection and can lower the offer or require repairs. Reroofing needs a City of Cheyenne permit.

faqs.q: Is my sale price public in Wyoming?
faqs.a: No. The sworn statement of consideration filed with the deed is confidential under W.S. 34-1-142 and is not a public record. The county uses it for statistical purposes.

faqs.q: When are property taxes due in Laramie County?
faqs.a: Half is payable by November 10 and half by May 10 of the next year. Interest on the first half is waived if you pay the full bill by December 31, and delinquent taxes accrue 18 percent interest per year.

faqs.q: Who do I call about a permit or a flood map in Cheyenne?
faqs.a: Call the Building Department at (307) 637-6265 for permits and Engineering Services at (307) 637-6268 for flood maps and base flood elevations. Planning and Development at (307) 637-6282 handles zoning, fences and setbacks.
